title: Hungarian Oak: Ancient Hungarian Oaks You Can Visit
meta_description: A large-leaved Balkan oak planted north on purpose. Glasgow's Suffragette Oak went into Kelvingrove Park in April 1918, days after women won the vote.
intro: Quercus frainetto is a large-leaved oak native to the Balkans and southeast Europe, reaching parks and streets further north only because someone planted it there on purpose. Its leaf is the giveaway, among the largest of any European oak and cut into many narrow lobes. Glasgow's grew from a single afternoon in April 1918: days after some British women won the vote, Louisa Lumsden planted it in Kelvingrove Park on behalf of four rival suffrage groups that agreed, for once, to plant a tree together. Krakow's, in Poland's oldest botanical garden, is 4.62 metres round. The Dutch register calls Arnhem's, in Park Zijpendaal, the tallest Hungarian oak measured in the Netherlands, leaning east from beeches that crowded it for a century. Warsaw's stands at the corner where Janusz Korczak ran his orphanage until 1942, and carries his name.
